title: FRM Foundations, Lesson 12: Four things you can do with a risk - avoid, reduce, transfer, retain
subtitle: Hedging is not always right, and leaving a risk in place is not always wrong
whyItMatters: Identifying and measuring a risk only means something if it leads to a decision. These four options are the entire decision space, and picking the wrong tool costs money in a way that does not show up immediately: hedging something you should have kept means paying a fee to shed the very thing you are being paid to carry.
openingQuestion: A commercial bank earns its living mainly from the spread between deposit and lending rates. How should it handle the credit risk in its loan book?
openingOptions: Transfer all of it out through credit derivatives so the book is risk-free
Retain most of it and manage it, because that is the risk of the trade
Avoid it entirely by lending only against a third-party guarantee
Reduce it as far as possible whatever the cost of doing so
explanation: Credit risk is the core business risk of a commercial bank - the risk premium inside the lending rate is its revenue. Transferring all of it out means handing that entire premium to someone else and keeping a business with no income stream. The right choice is to retain, but to retain under control: concentration limits, underwriting standards, provisions and capital. Transfer is for the portion beyond appetite, not for the core.

diagram.label: The risk is identified and measured
Is it inside our core competence - are we paid to carry it?
If yes: RETAIN and control · If no: REDUCE, TRANSFER or AVOID
Weigh the cost of the tool against the risk it actually deals with

realWorldExample.company: An airline hedging fuel and currency
realWorldExample.description: An airline hedging the fuel price is damping volatility in something outside its competence - it has no edge in forecasting crude. But the same airline hedging all of the currency risk on its ticket revenue is a different matter: if competitors do not hedge, a move in the exchange rate costs it the fare advantage at exactly the moment the competition gains one.

quiz.question: Scenario: hedging a risk costs 8bn a year, while the expected loss from that risk is 3bn a year. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: Consider retaining it, unless the tail is heavy enough
Hedge now, since removing risk is always worth it
Avoid it by stopping the activity that creates it
Transfer via insurance, always cheaper than derivatives
quiz.explanation: Paying 8bn to avoid an average loss of 3bn is a loss of 5bn a year on expected value alone. Hedging can still be the right call, but the reason has to be the tail - when a single bad year is heavy enough to threaten survival, paying the premium is rational. If the tail is not that heavy, retaining is cheaper. Insurance is not automatically cheaper than a derivative, and closing the activity forfeits its profit alongside its risk.

quiz.question: When is avoiding a risk the right choice rather than reducing or transferring it?
options: When the hedge costs more than the expected annual loss
When the activity does not create enough value to justify the risk
When there is no derivative instrument matching that risk
When regulators have written no specific rule for the activity
quiz.explanation: Avoidance means no longer doing the activity, so it is only right when the activity itself is not worth doing once the risk has been fully counted. An expensive hedge says a different instrument should be chosen; it does not say the business should be abandoned - those are two separate questions. The absence of a matching derivative points toward controls or insurance instead, and the absence of a specific rule is not a reason to exit either.

quiz.question: How does hedging differ from speculating, when both use derivatives?
options: Hedges always make money while speculation can lose
Hedges use only forwards, speculation only options
A hedge offsets an existing position, speculation creates one
Hedging is done by companies, speculation by funds
quiz.explanation: The same forward contract is a hedge for a company that owes money in a foreign currency and a speculation for someone who owes nothing. The distinction lies in the underlying position rather than in the instrument - which is also why over-hedging quietly turns into speculation. A hedge can certainly lose money, both forwards and options serve either purpose, and funds hedge while corporates take views, so the identity of the user settles nothing.

quiz.question: Why does transferring a risk through insurance not mean the risk has disappeared?
options: Because regulators do not recognise insurance as risk mitigation
Because an insurance contract can always be cancelled midway
Because the premium always exceeds the actual loss many times over
Because it becomes counterparty risk on the insurer instead
quiz.explanation: Transfer does not erase a risk, it changes its type: you now depend on the insurer still being able to pay when the event occurs. That matters most for systemic events, precisely because those are the moments when many claims arrive at once. Regulators do recognise insurance as mitigation within limits, contracts cannot generally be torn up mid-term at the insurer's convenience, and premiums exceed expected loss by a margin rather than by a multiple of several times.

quiz.question: What do all four risk-handling options have in common?
options: Each weighs the cost paid against the risk actually dealt with
Each one reduces the total amount of risk the organisation carries
Each requires board approval before it can be carried out
Each applies only to market risk and to credit risk
quiz.explanation: Retaining is a decision with its own price, and so is avoidance - dropping an activity drops its profit too. All four are trade-offs, so the question is always what is being spent to deal with which part of the risk, rather than how to make the risk as small as possible. Retention does not reduce total risk at all, none of the four is universally a board matter, and all four apply to operational and strategic risk as readily as to market and credit.

practicePrompt.question: An investment bank is considering hedging all the credit risk in its underwriting book - the core business it charges fees for. Which choice makes sense?
options: Retain deliberately, because that is the risk the firm is paid to carry
Transfer it all through CDS, since less risk is always the right direction
Avoid it entirely, because credit risk is outside the bank's competence
Reduce it with internal controls, as that is the cheapest tool available
practicePrompt.explanation: Avoid, reduce, transfer and retain are the whole decision space, and the most expensive mistake is assuming that reducing risk is always good. Underwriting is an activity the bank charges fees for PRECISELY BECAUSE it carries credit risk over the distribution window; hedging that away hands back the entire reason clients pay the fee. Retaining deliberately is not the same as retaining by neglect: it comes with limits, allocated economic capital, and an escalation process. Risk inside the core competence should be kept; what is worth transferring is risk where the firm has no edge at all.

keyTakeaways: Four options: avoid (exit the activity), reduce (controls), transfer (hedge, insure), retain (accept deliberately)
Risk inside the core competence should be RETAINED - it is what the firm is paid to carry
Transfer swaps the original risk for counterparty risk, which is especially dangerous in systemic events
Whether a hedge is right turns on having an underlying position to offset, not on the instrument used

summary.keyIdea: Measuring a risk is only half the job; the other half is choosing what to do about it. These four options are the entire decision space, and the most expensive mistake is assuming that reducing risk is always good.

application.message: For each significant risk in your portfolio, write down which of the four you have chosen - and why. A risk with no clear answer is usually one being retained without anyone ever deciding to retain it.

sections.text: Once a risk has been identified and measured, there are exactly four things you can do with it. The hard part is not listing them but knowing which one is right - and resisting the reflex that less risk is always better.
The filtering question: are we paid to carry it?

An organisation exists because it bears certain risks better than others do. A bank is paid to carry credit risk; an insurer is paid to carry mortality and accident risk. Those risks should not be transferred away - transferring them hands back the revenue. Risk outside the core competence, such as currency exposure for a manufacturer, is where hedging belongs.

Retaining deliberately is nothing like forgetting. Deliberate retention means the risk has been measured, compared against appetite, given capital, and assigned to someone who monitors it. Most of the risks that cause the heaviest damage are the ones nobody ever decided to keep - they were simply there, because nobody asked.
Transfer swaps one risk for another

Buying insurance or signing a derivative does not make a risk vanish, it converts the original risk into counterparty risk. For ordinary events that is a good trade. For systemic events it deserves more caution, because that is exactly when many parties claim at once and the protection seller is under pressure too.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: A hedge does not erase risk, it swaps price risk for basis risk. The right question is not whether risk remains, but whether what remains is smaller and more predictable.
